video_title: The Next Bull Market Is Hiding in Plain Sight
gist: Blockchain Capital GPs Spencer and Alex argue crypto is at the 2003-2004 point of the internet S-curve: infrastructure is overbuilt and cheap, value has structurally shifted from protocols to applications (2025 was the first year app-layer fees beat infrastructure fees), and the stablecoin flywheel is the engine. Their headline math: every $1B of net-new stablecoin issuance generates ~$122B of on-chain economic activity and ~$19M of recurring downstream on-chain protocol revenue per year, which at $2T of stablecoins by 2030 implies a 2,000x multiple on today's app-layer revenue base. They also map the crypto cycle onto AI's alt-lab financing bubble and lay out how tokenized equities actually reach trillions.

insights.claim: Buy-and-burn tokenomics, pioneered by MKR, remains the dominant value-accrual model in 2026 with the newest leading projects (Hyperliquid, Lighter, Venice) all adopting it despite years of criticism that it is capital-inefficient.
insights.speaker: David (host, Bankless)
insights.so_what: Token models that promise reinvestment over buybacks are still fighting an uphill battle; screen new token launches for an explicit burn commitment as a proxy for team seriousness.
insights.quote: here we are in 2026 and the best projects are still doing the buy and burn model. 100% works.

insights.claim: Protocols buy back and burn because token-holder legal rights remain undefined until the Clarity Act passes, making a hard-coded burn the only credible commitment device available to teams.
insights.speaker: Spencer (GP, Blockchain Capital)
insights.so_what: Passage of the Clarity Act is a catalyst that could legitimize dividend/reinvestment models and re-rate tokens that currently get no credit for retained cash flows.

insights.claim: Very few crypto protocols have demonstrated an ability to identify an adjacent opportunity and expand into it effectively, which is why token holders now prefer buybacks to reinvested cash flows.
insights.speaker: Spencer (GP, Blockchain Capital)
insights.so_what: Treat protocol 'expansion into adjacencies' announcements as a negative signal by default unless the team has a prior track record of successful product extension.

insights.claim: Crypto tokens function as a lemon market, so high-quality projects must burn their own token simply to differentiate themselves from the bad ones — a distortion that would disappear if the average token quality rose.
insights.speaker: David (host, Bankless)
insights.so_what: The buyback premium is a quality-signalling tax, not a valuation fundamental; as regulation and token quality improve, that premium should compress.
insights.quote: it's been a bit bit of a lemon market and so the people that are serious about their token have to buy back and burn their token just to show that they're better than the rest

insights.claim: Alex predicts buy-and-burn will not be the dominant crypto operating model in five years, because no venture investor would ever want a fast-growing Series A company to pay out a dividend instead of reinvesting.
insights.speaker: Alex (GP, Blockchain Capital)
insights.so_what: Protocols that build durable reinvestment capability early could compound faster than serial burners once the market allows it; today's burn-obsession is a timing artifact.
insights.quote: but in 5 years from now, I'd be surprised if if if that's still the dominant operating model

themes.theme: Crypto's S-curve: we're at the internet's 2003

insights.claim: Alex places crypto at the equivalent of 2003-2004 for the internet: the block-space equivalent of the broadband shift has just happened, the mobile-explosion analogue has not, and crypto is still on the flat part of the S-curve.
insights.speaker: Alex (GP, Blockchain Capital)
insights.so_what: Implies the biggest adoption-driven repricing is ahead, not behind — a case for accumulating during the attention drought rather than waiting for confirmation.
insights.quote: my perspective is we're in like 2003, 2004. We we've just had that like shift to to broadband um and and we're maybe like pre the mobile boom and so like we're in the flat part of the S-curve.

insights.claim: Alex argues the adoption clock for crypto should start at Ethereum's launch in 2015 rather than Bitcoin's, putting the 'internet of assets' roughly 10-11 years in — the same point at which the internet was still clunky and bandwidth constrained.
insights.speaker: Alex (GP, Blockchain Capital)
insights.so_what: Reframes 'crypto has had 17 years and failed' bear arguments; the correct comparison window makes current traction look early rather than disappointing.

insights.claim: There are roughly 700 million crypto holders globally but only about 10% are on-chain active users, meaning the conversion funnel from holder to user is the single largest untapped adoption lever.
insights.speaker: Alex (GP, Blockchain Capital)
insights.so_what: Applications that convert passive holders into active users address a 630M-person addressable gap — a better bet than acquiring net-new holders.
insights.quote: There's 700 million, you know, some odd uh crypto holders out there.

insights.claim: The usable consumer crypto stack — embedded wallets, social recovery, spending limits, familiar authentication, account abstraction — is only about three years old, which explains why mass-market applications haven't landed yet rather than any failure of demand.
insights.speaker: Alex (GP, Blockchain Capital)
insights.so_what: The lag between primitive maturity and breakout consumer apps is a normal 2-4 year build cycle; the 2026-2028 app cohort is the one to underwrite.
insights.quote: the consumer stack in crypto is 3 years old

insights.claim: This crypto bear market is structurally different because it has more positive catalysts than any prior one — the Genius Act, expected Clarity Act, serious institutional entry, and use cases like prediction markets and stablecoins that grew straight through the drawdown.
insights.speaker: Alex (GP, Blockchain Capital)
insights.so_what: Secular growth persisting through a bear is the tell that the cycle low is fundamentally different; use price weakness as entry rather than confirmation of thesis failure.
insights.quote: Like we've never had a bare market with this many positive catalysts, right?

insights.claim: Alex frames AI's attention capture as a trap rather than a signal — asset prices are down and attention has shifted away, but crypto has already crossed the hard part of the chasm and is 'kindling waiting for the fire'.
insights.speaker: Alex (GP, Blockchain Capital)
insights.so_what: The clearest stated buy-the-neglect argument in the episode; positions crypto exposure as a contrarian allocation against the AI-attention consensus.
insights.quote: this is a distraction it's an absolute trap and like we're headed for that inflection point

insights.claim: For the first time in crypto's history institutions are leaning into the asset class while prices are down, meaning their entry is driven by their own merit-based analysis rather than narrative chasing at price highs.
insights.speaker: David (host, Bankless), citing Alex
insights.so_what: Institutional inflows decoupled from price momentum are stickier; watch institutional on-chain deployment as a leading rather than lagging indicator.
insights.quote: for the first time ever institutions are leaning in while prices are down

insights.claim: Spencer attributes OG crypto pessimism to path dependency and the startup-IPO psychological pattern rather than fundamentals: sentiment would be entirely different if the industry had reached today's state on a linear path instead of from higher prices.
insights.speaker: Spencer (GP, Blockchain Capital)
insights.so_what: Separate sentiment signal from fundamental signal — native-community pessimism here is a price-path artifact and not evidence of deteriorating fundamentals.
insights.quote: If that line was like a nice steady linear path to where we are today, sentiment would be completely different. But there is some path dependency there because we were once higher than we are today.

insights.claim: The decentralization properties that attracted cypherpunks — neutral networks not controlled by any company or government — are the same properties institutions value as a trust substrate, so permissioned regulated products and permissionless base layers are not mutually exclusive.
insights.speaker: Alex (GP, Blockchain Capital)
insights.so_what: Bitcoin and ETH retain a monetary/escape-valve bid even as the regulated stack grows on top of them; the two demand sources compound rather than compete.
insights.quote: that cipher punk dream is alive. It's just not allowed.

themes.theme: Fat protocol to fat app: value moves up the stack

insights.claim: In 2021 over 70% of the fees crypto users paid went to infrastructure, and 2025 was the first year application-layer fees surpassed infrastructure fees — a structural shift of value up the stack.
insights.speaker: Spencer (GP, Blockchain Capital)
insights.so_what: The single most quantified claim for rotating from L1/L2 tokens into application tokens; it dates the crossover precisely to 2025.
insights.quote: I think it was 2025 was the first time that application layer fees surpassed infrastructure fees.

insights.claim: The fat protocol thesis was valid only until roughly 2022-2023 and was killed by Solana making block space abundant, ending the scarcity that made constrained-block-space protocols valuable.
insights.speaker: David (host, Bankless)
insights.so_what: Anyone still underwriting L1 tokens on the fat protocol thesis is using a framework its own proponents now date as expired.

insights.claim: Alex's reformulation is 'thin protocols but massive markets' — a small rake on a global financial system an order of magnitude larger than today still produces protocol revenue that would look fat by current standards.
insights.speaker: Alex (GP, Blockchain Capital)
insights.so_what: Reconciles low take rates with large absolute protocol revenue; the right variable to model is market expansion, not rake compression.
insights.quote: it's thin protocols but massive markets

insights.claim: Alex argues the market is currently too negative on crypto infrastructure because blocks are empty, but that abundant cheap block space is the prerequisite for the application wave rather than evidence of failure.
insights.speaker: Alex (GP, Blockchain Capital)
insights.so_what: Sets up a potential mean-reversion trade in beaten-down infrastructure tokens once app demand starts filling the overbuilt capacity.
insights.quote: we're probably a little bit too negative on on the infrastructure at the moment because a lot of the blocks are empty

insights.claim: Alt-L1s at roughly $5B FDV may already be priced for huge future adoption while protocol fees alone cannot sustain the business, forcing them to find another way to create value.
insights.speaker: Alex (GP, Blockchain Capital)
insights.so_what: Concrete valuation screen: L1s with multi-billion FDV and no application strategy are structurally short of a business model.
insights.quote: if you're at like 5 billion FTB now like you you you might already be at the market cap implied by like huge future adoption

themes.theme: AI alt-labs rhyme with 2018 crypto L1s

insights.claim: Alex maps AI alt-labs onto 2018-era L1 launches almost line for line: research thesis and elite talent equal a whitepaper and founding team, model benchmarks equal testnet TPS, hyperscaler distribution equals exchange listings, and private valuation equals token price.
insights.speaker: Alex (GP, Blockchain Capital)
insights.so_what: A ready-made pattern-recognition template for underwriting AI lab financings using crypto's 2018 blowup as the base rate.

insights.claim: Because AI valuations are private rather than a real-time sentiment gauge, an alt-lab unwind will look like down rounds, structured financings, acquihires and hyperscaler consolidation rather than the 90%-in-a-month token collapse crypto experienced.
insights.speaker: Alex (GP, Blockchain Capital)
insights.so_what: Investors should not expect a visible AI 'crash' signal; the deflation will be slow, opaque and expressed in deal structure, not marks.
insights.quote: an unwind of that like alt lab thesis you know probably looks you know much more like you know down round structured financings aqua hires like talent migrating to to other opportunities maybe consolidation

insights.claim: Model weights are becoming a commodity but the harness around them is not, so durable AI moats will form at the application layer in domains with feedback loops, proprietary data and zero tolerance for hallucination — semiconductor manufacturing being the example given.
insights.speaker: Alex (GP, Blockchain Capital)
insights.so_what: Directs AI dollars toward vertical application companies with data feedback loops rather than toward marginal frontier-lab exposure.
insights.quote: weights are are um you know are largely going to be a commodity uh but the harness is is certainly not

insights.claim: Alex expects frontier labs to absorb simple, generalizable application categories like accounting but not complex specialized verticals where solving more customer problems compounds domain knowledge that doesn't generalize back to the model.
insights.speaker: Alex (GP, Blockchain Capital)
insights.so_what: A concrete rule for which AI app startups are at risk of being absorbed by the labs versus which can defend a niche.

insights.claim: Spencer argues crypto investors are unusually well prepared for AI because crypto has never had software moats — its entire stack is forkable open source — so the AI industry's 'software moats are dead' reckoning is a question crypto has been answering for a decade.
insights.speaker: Spencer (GP, Blockchain Capital)
insights.so_what: Crypto-native value-accrual frameworks (liquidity, network effects, distribution, brand) transfer directly to AI application underwriting.
insights.quote: You guys had software modes. We've never had software remotes.

themes.theme: The stablecoin flywheel and the $19M per $1B metric

insights.claim: Blockchain Capital is the only venture investor in all three major stablecoin issuers — Tether, Circle and Paxos — with all three investments made almost a decade ago, an example of the 'ten years to make an overnight success' pattern.
insights.speaker: Spencer (GP, Blockchain Capital)
insights.so_what: Establishes the speakers' informational edge on stablecoins and shows the 10-year lag between correct thesis and payoff in this sector.
insights.quote: we're the only venture investor in all three of the major stable coin issuers, Tether, Circle, and Paxos

insights.claim: Stablecoin supply sits at roughly $300 billion today and Spencer assigns over 90% confidence to reaching trillions by 2030, explicitly affirming $2 trillion within four years.
insights.speaker: Spencer (GP, Blockchain Capital)
insights.so_what: A ~7x supply forecast on a four-year horizon is the load-bearing assumption behind every downstream DeFi revenue estimate in this episode.
insights.quote: today we're at something like 300 billion. I have zero doubt in my mind that we're going to the trillions by 2030.

insights.claim: Stablecoin velocity runs around 120x, meaning the average on-chain stablecoin dollar turns over roughly 120 times per year — far above traditional payment network or M1 benchmarks.
insights.speaker: Spencer (GP, Blockchain Capital)
insights.so_what: Velocity is the proposed metric for proving on-chain financial infrastructure is genuinely more capital efficient; track it as the health indicator for the sector.
insights.quote: the velocity of stable coins, it's something like 120x, meaning that the average stable coin dollar turns over 120 times per year in the onchain economy

insights.claim: Spencer argues the common investor framing of stablecoins as a payments product is wrong: dollars that come on chain stay on chain with a high attach rate, and a little over half of net new issuance is immediately deployed as on-chain working capital into lending protocols and exchanges.
insights.speaker: Spencer (GP, Blockchain Capital)
insights.so_what: If stablecoins are a working-capital product rather than a payments rail, DeFi protocol revenue — not payment processors — is the correct downstream exposure.
insights.quote: They say stable coins are cool. They're a payments product. Like no, no, they're actually not a payments product

insights.claim: Blockchain Capital's own modelling finds that $1 billion of net new stablecoin issuance produces roughly $122 billion of on-chain economic activity and about $19 million of recurring downstream on-chain protocol revenue per year.
insights.speaker: Spencer (GP, Blockchain Capital)
insights.so_what: A directly usable multiplier: apply $19M per $1B of stablecoin growth to forecast aggregate DeFi revenue, then discount for efficiency gains that compress the ratio over time.
insights.quote: roughly a billion dollars of net new stable coin issuance produces about $19 million of downstream protocol revenue

insights.claim: Applying the $19M-per-$1B ratio to $2 trillion of additional stablecoin supply implies roughly 2,000x today's annual downstream protocol revenue accruing to on-chain applications, and Spencer notes the numbers stay extraordinary even if efficiency gains cut the ratio to $10M.
insights.speaker: Spencer (GP, Blockchain Capital) and David (host)
insights.so_what: The explicit bull case for DeFi blue-chip cash flows; the sensitivity analysis shows the thesis survives a ~50% haircut to the multiplier.
insights.quote: it's the fattest pitch of the game and a lot of people are taking their eye off the ball right now

insights.claim: The stablecoin revenue captured on chain — lending protocols, exchange protocols like Uniswap, Morpho vaults and derivatives venues — excludes the value captured by closed businesses such as Tether, Circle, Coinbase, Kraken and TRM, so the $19M figure understates total sector economics.
insights.speaker: Spencer (GP, Blockchain Capital)
insights.so_what: Identifies exactly which token categories are the levered plays on stablecoin growth: DEXes, lending markets and derivatives venues.

themes.theme: Tokenized equities and the token as shipping container

insights.claim: The stablecoin flywheel is now institutionally rather than retail driven, so each turn is larger than the last and it is pulling in tokenized equities, money market funds and treasuries alongside dollars.
insights.speaker: Spencer (GP, Blockchain Capital)
insights.so_what: Stablecoin growth is the leading indicator for the broader RWA wave; treat rising stablecoin float as a forward signal for tokenized-asset volume.

insights.claim: Alex compares the token to the standardized shipping container, which cut loading time by roughly 97% and reorganized global supply chains without changing the goods — the token is the standardized interface for economic rights that will do the same for finance.
insights.speaker: Alex (GP, Blockchain Capital)
insights.so_what: Frames the investable thesis as interface standardization rather than new asset creation; value accrues to whatever aggregates the standardized flow.
insights.quote: I think it was like a 97% reduction in like loading time um that that the standardized container produced.

insights.claim: Spencer argues private permissioned chains will not work because the entire value proposition of tokenization is pulling assets out of institutional silos so an open marketplace can competitively bid to service them — as opposed to phoning Charles Schwab for a limited, high-friction margin loan.
insights.speaker: Spencer (GP, Blockchain Capital)
insights.so_what: A direct bet against bank-consortium private chains and in favour of public-chain RWA venues capturing the tokenized asset flow.
insights.quote: in order to do that, you must pull them out of these private silos and you must put them on public infrastructure where other people can kind of compete to service those assets

insights.claim: Tokenized equities will follow stablecoins' two-wave pattern: wave one is frictionless international access to US stocks (uninteresting to already well-served American investors), and wave two — the larger prize — is programmability and composability such as competing lenders bidding to finance an on-chain equity portfolio.
insights.speaker: Spencer (GP, Blockchain Capital)
insights.so_what: Early tokenized-equity volume will be non-US retail; underwrite distribution into emerging markets first and composability infrastructure second.

insights.claim: The Xstocks model from Backed (acquired by Kraken) gives full permissionless DeFi composability but the holder owns a debt instrument tied to an SPV rather than the actual share, which is acceptable for retail but blocks the institutions holding billions from ever reaching trillions of tokenized equities.
insights.speaker: Spencer (GP, Blockchain Capital)
insights.so_what: Identifies true share ownership as the gating feature for institutional tokenized-equity scale; wrapper products cap out at retail-sized TAM.
insights.quote: But there is a serious downside to them, which is you do not own an actual share.

insights.claim: Spencer, who says he was relatively bearish on tokenized equities for years, has turned because the SEC is now pounding the table that they should happen — and he expects tens of trillions of equities to live in permissioned 'sidecars' running alongside, and ultimately accelerating, the permissionless chains.
insights.speaker: Spencer (GP, Blockchain Capital)
insights.so_what: A named view change from a decade-long RWA skeptic, driven by regulator posture — the clearest catalyst-based reason to raise tokenized-equity exposure now.
insights.quote: I've actually been relatively bearish on the notion of tokenized equities for some years.

themes.theme: BCAP: lessons from the first tokenized fund

insights.claim: Blockchain Capital tokenized Fund 3 on Ethereum in March 2017 at a deliberately small $10 million because it believed that if anyone was going to disrupt venture capital with blockchains it should be the firm itself; that fund is now roughly $1 billion in assets.
insights.speaker: Spencer (GP, Blockchain Capital)
insights.so_what: A nine-year track record proving tokenized funds can compound; the template other asset managers will copy as compliance infrastructure matures.
insights.quote: if anybody is going to go and disrupt this business and this industry using blockchains, it better be us

insights.claim: The BCAP token proved the access thesis with participants from roughly 80 different countries including a researcher in Antarctica, but the liquidity thesis stalled because a registered security cannot simply be listed on Uniswap for anyone to trade.
insights.speaker: Spencer (GP, Blockchain Capital)
insights.so_what: Access is the easy half of tokenization and liquidity is the hard half; regulated secondary-trading infrastructure is the bottleneck worth funding.
insights.quote: we had participants from like 80 different countries, including, by the way, a researcher up in Antarctica

insights.claim: Because the tokenized fund is a permanent capital vehicle with no end of life — holders exit by selling the token rather than redeeming — Blockchain Capital can hold portfolio companies indefinitely and is never a forced seller, which mattered for Circle, Paxos and Tether that only had their moment in year ten.
insights.speaker: Spencer (GP, Blockchain Capital)
insights.so_what: Tokenization converts the standard 10-15 year VC lockup into permanent capital — a structural advantage that could reshape how venture funds are raised.

insights.claim: Aave's V4 spoke architecture has made it possible for a regulated tokenized fund like BCAP to create a lending market against its own token in about a day, a setup that was previously infeasible for non-crypto-native collateral.
insights.speaker: Alex (GP, Blockchain Capital)
insights.so_what: Modular lending architectures that extend to regulated RWA collateral are the unlock for institutional on-chain credit; watch V4 spoke deployments as the adoption metric.
insights.quote: that conversation has been, oh, you know, that'll take like a day to set up basically
